q: If we could travel at the speed of light, how would time perception actually change?
How would time change if we traveled at light speed?
What happens to time at the speed of light?
How does time dilation work at light speed?
What would time look like at the speed of light?
How does traveling at light speed affect time?
a: According to Einstein's theory of relativity, if we could travel at the speed of light, time would behave very differently. As an object approaches the speed of light, time dilation occurs — time slows down relative to a stationary observer. At the speed of light itself, time would effectively stop from the perspective of a stationary observer. This means that if you traveled at light speed to a distant star and back, you would experience no passage of time, while everyone else on Earth would have aged normally during your journey. This phenomenon, called time dilation, has been confirmed by experiments with atomic clocks on airplanes and satellites. The closer you get to the speed of light, the more pronounced the effect becomes. At 90% of light speed, time would pass at about 44% the normal rate. At 99% of light speed, time would pass at about 14% the normal rate. This creates fascinating possibilities for space travel — a journey that would take thousands of years from Earth's perspective could be completed in just a few years from the traveler's perspective. However, it's important to note that objects with mass cannot actually reach the speed of light, as they would require infinite energy to accelerate to that speed. Only massless particles like photons can travel at light speed, and for them, time does not pass at all — from a photon's perspective, it is emitted and absorbed simultaneously, regardless of the distance traveled.
